entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Darius II (reigned 423–404 BCE), born Ochus, ascended to the throne of the Achaemenid Empire amidst a period of political instability following the death of his father, Artaxerxes I. His nearly two-decade reign was characterized by efforts to maintain central authority over the vast Persian Empire, contend with powerful satraps, and strategically intervene in the affairs of the Greek city-states during the Peloponnesian War. While not a conqueror, Darius II's policies significantly shaped the geopolitical landscape of the Eastern Mediterranean, ensuring Persian influence remained a formidable force in the Classical world.

His path to power was marked by intrigue and violence; after his father's death, several half-brothers briefly held the throne before Ochus, supported by the eunuch Artaxares and his powerful wife Parysatis, consolidated his rule as Darius II. Internally, his reign saw persistent challenges from ambitious satraps, including the notable revolt of Pissuthnes of Lydia (c. 414 BCE) and the rebellion of his own brother Artoxares (c. 410 BCE), which Darius II suppressed with varying degrees of success. Externally, he skillfully exploited the internecine conflicts of the Greek world, particularly by providing substantial financial backing to Sparta against Athens from 413 BCE, effectively turning the tide of the Peloponnesian War in Sparta's favor and reasserting Persian control over the Greek cities of Ionia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Darius II's strategic intervention in the Peloponnesian War fundamentally altered its outcome, reasserting Persian dominance in the Aegean and setting the stage for future Greco-Persian relations, including the King's Peace. His reign also saw the preservation of the Achaemenid imperial structure despite significant internal challenges.
